POINT-BY-POINT RESPONSE TO REVIEWERS’ COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author): with expertise in cancer immunology, STING
“Gong and colleagues provide a well written, well developed and rigorously performed study identifying BATF2 as a tumor suppressor gene acting via feed-forward activation of the STING/IFN-I/Tgd pathway, with BATF2 transcription/expression negatively modulated by local (dietary) glutamine concentrations. Increased intrinsic expression of BATF2 in tumors leads to enhanced anti-tumor T cell fitness and improved tumor growth control in vivo across multiple mouse (transplantable and inducible) HNSCC tumor models, while deficiency of BATF2 in tumors results in a pro-tumor TIME characterized by enriched M2 TAM and reduced Type-1 T cell content. Furthermore, BATF2-KO mice exhibited greater intrinsic susceptibility to tumor initiation/growth/progression in multiple model systems. Overall, the presented data support the ability of BATF2 to sustain optimal fitness of the STING signaling pathway within the TME and suggest that future therapeutic targeting to reinforce BATF2 expression and/or to reduce glutamine metabolism may improve (immune)therapeutic outcomes in the HNSCC (cancer) setting.”
Response: We appreciate the insightful comments from Reviewer #1 and have performed additional experiments to enhance the rigor of this study. Please refer to our point-by-point response below.
1. “The report is interesting and informative and my only minor concerns reflect: For the data presented in Fig. 5k and 5l where I would request that the authors redraft the Fig. 5l tumor growth curves with the same y-axis range (i.e., 1500 mm2) as was used for Fig. 5k. Also, the fact that the glutamine diet negated the significance of response to STING agonist may be true, but this does not appear to provide a survival advantage based on the perceived trajectories for tumor growth in Figs. 5k/l. Can the authors provide Kaplan-Meier plots and the relevant statistical analyses to support or refute the impact of the glutamine diet?”
Response 1: Thank you for this thoughtful suggestion. To directly compare the impact of an isocaloric, glutamine-rich diet on tumor growth using this model, we repeated the experiment so that all mice were treated and monitored in the same cohort and included the new data in New Fig. 5k. Consistent with our prior submission, we found that intra-tumoral injection of CDA was sufficient to reduce tumor burden when mice were on a regular diet. A glutamine-rich diet dampened host response to STING stimulation, as shown by the diminished tumor control by CDA. Without any STING agonists, tumors grew more aggressively in mice fed with an isocaloric, glutamine-rich diet than those on a regular diet (New Fig. 5k, Line 374-378). We compared the Kaplan-Meier curves and found that a glutamine-enriched diet was associated with inferior overall survival at baseline. STING stimulation improved overall survival for mice on a regular diet. However, STING stimulation failed to offer any meaningful protection in mice on an isocaloric, glutamine-rich diet (New Supplementary Fig. 7g, Line 385-388). In addition, to directly evaluate the effect of glutamine metabolism in tumor response to STING agonists, we treated mice with a prodrug of 6-diazo-5-oxo-L-norleucine, JHU083, which specifically inhibits glutaminase. JHU083 did not further improve the tumor response to STING agonists when mice were fed a regular diet. However, inhibition of glutamine metabolism in mice on a glutamine-rich diet sensitized cancers that were refractory to STING agonists to CDA (New Fig. 5l-m, Line 388-393).
2. “Per Fig. 5m/n, the major difference in the TIME impacted by the glutamine diet appears to reflect presence of CXCR5+ B cells under constitutive glutamine concentrations in the TME. The authors should provide data for comparative levels of CXCL13 expression (including which cells are producing via scRNAseq) in the TME under both conditions. Also, since B cells are a canonical component of mature tertiary lymphoid structures, are TLS prevalent in control tumors but devoid in mice fed the glutamine diet? Please discuss and provide supportive data is available.”
Response 2: Thank you for this insightful question. We first performed additional histologic and immunohistochemical staining of CD20, trying to identify TLS. In agreement with previous studies (reviewed in PMID: 37809103), which showed that most syngeneic cell lines implanted s.c. do not develop TLS naturally due to the rapid growth, we did not observe apparent mature TLS in this study. To determine whether the increase in B-cell infiltration post STING stimulation shown in the single-cell analysis can be validated, we quantified CD20 staining of tumors from different treatment groups. We found that STING stimulation expanded B-cells in the tumors grown in mice on a regular diet but failed to increase B-cell infiltration in tumors grown in mice on a glutamine-rich diet (New Supplementary Fig. 7l-m, Line 417-424). Then, we examined the single-cell data set to evaluate B-cell signatures and Cxcl13. We quantified the fold change in gene expression for B-cell and plasma-cell markers, including CD19, Cxcr5, Ms4a1 (CD20), CD79a, Sdc1 (CD138), Igkc, Ighm, Ighd, Fcer2a (CD23), Cr2 (CD21/CD35), and Sell (CD62L). Besides the lineage markers, we included some functional markers because marginal zone B-cells are defined as CD93-IghdlowIghmhighCD23lowCD21high and follicular B-cells are defined as CD93-IghdhighIghmlowCD62L+CD23highCD21mid. We found that STING stimulation is more prominently promoting the upregulation of multiple functional B-cell subset markers in tumors grown in mice on a regular diet than those grown in mice on a glutamine-rich diet (New Supplementary Fig. 7l-m, Line 417-424). This single-cell data set did not identify Cxcl13 in any clusters. Cxcl13 is mainly produced by follicular dendritic cells and follicular helper T-cells, which are usually more prominent in mature TLS. Syngeneic models typically do not produce TLS. Cxcl13 is the main chemokine to guide B cells into TLS. However, B-cells also respond to other chemokine gradients, such as Cxcl10, to infiltrate into the TME. We did observe an expansion of Cxcl10high myeloid cell subset in response to STING stimulation in mice on a regular diet (Fig. 5n-o). Overall, the STING activation promotes the infiltration of B-cell subsets with transitional features of marginal zone and follicular B-cells into the TME. Glutamine dampens STING-mediated B-cell infiltration.
3. “The discussion is rather short overall and more discussion for practical means by which BATF2 might be pharmacologically upregulated in the TME for therapeutic gain is recommended. Can the authors speak to known promoters of BATF2 or epigenetic agents that might be targeted with known in clinic drugs for testing in prospective translational studies (alone or in combination with immunotherapeutic agents)? Such discussion would add to the merit of the report.”
Response 3: Thank you for this insightful suggestion. To assess the potential for reversing BATF2 inhibition through pharmacologic approaches, in the same experiment shown in Fig. 5k, we also included two additional groups that received intra-tumoral injection of CDA and a glutaminase inhibitor, JHU083. One of these groups was on a regular diet, and the other was on an isocaloric glutamine-rich diet. Interestingly, although JHU083 did not further improve the anti-tumor efficacy of CDA in the regular diet group, it significantly improved tumor control in mice on a glutamine-rich diet (New Fig. 5l-m, Line 387-393). EZH2 is a key enzyme that methylates H3K27. Recent studies show that inhibition of EZH2 potentiates IFN-I, which supports this mechanistic link. Thus, in addition to improving the pharmacokinetic properties of STING agonists, the development of strategies to overcome BATF2-dependence, such as inhibition of EZH2 or glutamine metabolism, is promising to sensitize cancers to STING-mediated immune priming approaches. We have expanded the discussion section and included more details (Line 585-596, Line 607-621, Line 622-649).
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author): with expertise in cancer immunology, IFNs
“Gong et al. identified BATF2 as a novel regulator of the STING-type I interferon axis. They show that BATF2 directly interacts with STING, thereby promoting downstream signaling and target gene expression. By integrating molecular and functional in vitro studies with in vivo experiments in transplantable tumor models, the authors conclude that BATF2 is a tumor suppressor in HNSCC and that loss of BATF2 expression is a mechanism of immune evasion, as it impairs STING signaling in tumor cells.”
1. “Comment: The BATF2-STING axis is a novel and very interesting finding. However, additional (control) experiments are needed to clearly demonstrate that BATF2 is a tumor suppressor and that downregulation of BATF2 in tumor cells is of relevance in immune evasion of HNSCC.”
Response 1: Thank you for your thoughtful suggestion. We measured the transcription levels of Batf2 in syngeneic murine HNSCC cell lines, including MOC2-E6/E7, NOOC1, and NOOC2. We found that MOC2-E6/E7 exhibited the lowest endogenous level of Batf2 expression, while NOOC2 showed high endogenous levels of Batf2 expression (New Supplementary Fig. 9a, Line 456-459). In addition to the Batf2-expressing MOC2-E6/E7 model we included in the original submission (Fig. 6), we generated new stable Batf2-deficient NOOC2 cells with its empty vector control (New Supplementary Fig. 9l, Line 523-525). In agreement with our previous findings, Batf2-deficient tumors grew significantly more aggressively (New Supplementary Fig. 9l-m, Line 523-526).
2. “Comments on the role of BATF2 as novel tumor suppressor: So far, there is no evidence for a tumor-suppressor function of BATF2 in HNSCC, as the manuscript does not compare the in situ expression of BATF2 between cancer cells and normal squamous cells. What is shown in Fig. 1f? Are BATF2 levels in cancer cells, or are the BATF2 levels for the entire tissue core presented? Since BATF2 can also be induced by interferon-gamma, the correlation between BATF2 and CD8 could be driven by IFN-γ release from CD8 T cells. In this case, HNSCC tumor cells may not lose BATF2 expression but rather acquire it due to signals from the microenvironment. Moreover, several single-cell RNA sequencing datasets for HNSCC are available (including those from different disease stages, e.g., PMID: 36828832), where BATF2 expression in cancer cells could be analyzed and plotted. The authors analyzed BATF2 expression in tissue cores from 200 patients with a median follow-up of 60 months. Is there any association between BATF2 expression and survival or disease progression? If BATF2 is a strong tumor suppressor, patients with high BATF2 expression should have a significantly better outcome. Finally, introducing BATF2 as a general tumor suppressor is an overstatement, as the authors focused their studies solely on HNSCC.”
Response 2: Thank you for raising this thoughtful point. We appreciate the importance of strengthening human specimen studies and included new analyses using three additional independent cohorts of clinical specimens. A common caveat of analyzing human OPMD specimens is the often lack of longitudinal monitoring, including the referenced study (PMID: 36828832), where leukoplakia of unknown malignant transformation potential is included. To substantiate the role of BATF2 in suppressing tumor initiation, we first identified patients who had OPMD progressing into HNSCC despite complete surgical removal of the OPMD. We performed BATF2 staining on the paired longitudinal specimens and found that BATF2 expression levels were lower in paired HNSCC than in OPMD (New Fig. 1f-g, Line 161-163). Next, to directly assess whether the expression levels of BATF2 in fresh human oral squamous cell carcinoma specimens regulate their response to IFN agonists, we procured fresh human oral squamous cell carcinomas from eight patients. We trisected the tissue into three pieces of comparable size. The first piece was injected with PBS ex vivo, the second piece was injected with 5.0 μg CDA, and the third piece was formalin fixed and integrated into a tissue microarray (New Fig. 1h-i, Line 163-172). We performed qPCR using tissue homogenates and normalized the levels of IFNB1 by PTPRC, the latter of which encodes CD45. We quantified BATF2 staining using Aperio Imagescope and generated BATF2 scores. Then, we performed a Spearman correlation analysis between BATF2 scores and normalized IFNB1 expression and identified a strong positive correlation with a r-value of 0.86 (**p<0.01) (New Fig. 1h-i, Line 163-172).
Our previous Fig.1f (current Fig. 1e) showed cancer-specific BATF2 expression in the upper panel and TME-specific BATF2 expression in the lower panel. This TMA was based on a clinical cohort collected through the former University of Michigan (UMich) Head and Neck SPORE, which ended in 2012. The follow-up was stopped after the grant ended, which made the follow-up data complex and not ideal. Over a decade has passed, and the statisticians for the UMich SPORE also left. However, we appreciate the value of assessing the prognostic role of BATF2, given its tumor-inhibitory role. Thus, we resorted to five TCGA data sets that include HNSCC (n=522, *p=0.034), high-grade serous carcinoma (OV, n=303, *p=0.0181), sarcoma (SARC, n=260, *p=0.0208), skin cutaneous melanoma (SKCM, n=471, **p=0.00106), and stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD, n=415, *p=0.0428). We found that higher expression levels of BATF2 were positively correlated with patient outcomes (New Supplementary Fig. 1e-i, Line 154-158). The HNSCC TCGA data set does not have responder status for immunotherapy. Thus, we next examined four data sets that contained responder status to anti-PD1. We found that the responders among patients with STAD (****p<0.0001), SKCM (****p<0.0001), bladder squamous cell carcinoma (BLCA, *p=0.02), or non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC, ****p<0.0001) showed significantly higher levels of BATF2 expression than non-responders (New Supplementary Fig. 1j-m, Line 173-177). Overall, these new exciting data show that BATF2 inhibits the initiation of HNSCC and promotes anti-tumor immunity in human specimens.
3. “Comments on the BATF2-STING axis in human squamous cell carcinoma cell lines. To demonstrate that BATF2 impacts STING signaling in carcinoma cells, the authors had to overexpress both BATF2 and, notably, STING, since synthetic STING agonists do not induce “… robust IFN-I activation” (author statement, lines 205-207, page 10). Even in cell lines with high endogenous STING levels (Fig. 3F, cell lines UMSCC108, UMSCC49), STING must be overexpressed to achieve pathway activation. This raises the question: how relevant is the BATF2-STING axis in squamous cell carcinoma if STING cannot be activated upon transfection with synthetic agonists? This suggests that activation of endogenous STING is defective even in the presence of high BATF2 levels.”
Response 3: We appreciate this thoughtful comment. We and others have shown that cancer cells have evolved multiple mechanisms to suppress the STING-TBK1-IFN pathway, such as promoting the turnover of STING and sequestering STING away from interacting with TBK1. This pathway is central for the immune sensing of HNSCC, which is likely why the tumors need multiple mechanisms to dampen this pathway. The regulation of this pathway is highly relevant for the following reasons.
(a) During tumor initiation, when immune surveillance determines the outcomes of epithelial transformation, the proper activation of the innate immune pathways enables the maturation of antigen-presenting cells and subsequent cross-priming of T-cells. Known oncogenes for HNSCC, such as SOX2 and HPV16 E7, potently shut down IFN-I production. To evaluate whether BATF2 helps to launch the IFN-I pathway before epithelial malignant transformation, we expressed BATF2 in normal oral epithelial NOM9-TK cells, which directly triggered the phosphorylation of TBK1 and STING, indicative of pathway activation (New Supplementary Fig. 3d, Line 234-240).
(b) In murine HNSCC cells, high Batf2 expression was also associated with elevated transcription levels of Ifnb1 (New Supplementary Fig. 9a and l, Line 456-459 and 523-525). In our previous submission, we showed that Batf2-expressing tumors are much more immunogenic (Fig. 6). To substantiate the physiological relevance of the Batf2-Sting pathway, we generated additional stable cell lines, including vector control Batf2-expressing and Batf2-expressing, Sting-deficient tumor cells. We found that cancer cell-specific Batf2-mediated tumor rejection completely depended on cancer cell expression of Sting because knocking down Sting abrogated Batf2-mediated protection (New Supplementary Fig. 9f-g, Line 473-477).
(c) Now we also show that HNSCC cells only showed a modest increase in the phosphorylation of TBK1 and STING with cGAMP transfection. However, the STING response was largely restored when we expressed BATF2 (New Supplementary Fig. 4h, Line 308-311).
(d) Although squamous cell carcinoma cells show a modest response to STING agonists, the magnitude of such differential responses can be amplified through myeloid cells, eventually controlling the infiltration of effector immune cells. To further characterize how cancer cell-specific expression of Batf2 impacts the effectors as a function of time, we implanted empty vector control and Batf2-expressing MOC2-E6/E7 cells, derived from a tumor model that has low endogenous levels of Batf2 expression (New Supplementary Fig. 9a, line 456-459), and analyzed tumor-infiltrating immune cells on Days 7, 14, and 21 post implantation. We found that Batf2-expressing tumors rapidly recruit CD11b+ myeloid cells that showed higher levels of phospho-Irf3 (New Fig. 6g, Line 477-488) and gd T-cells (New Fig. 6h, Line 477-488). At later time points, including Days 14 and 21, cancer cell-specific Batf2 expression resulted in an increased infiltration of CD8+ T-cells (New Fig. 6i, Line 477-488), in agreement with our analysis presented in the original submission (Fig. 6j-m).
4. “Comments on silencing of BATF2 by glutamine: The authors conducted several in vitro studies to demonstrate that glutamine, by enhancing oxidative phosphorylation, leads to the epigenetic silencing of BATF2 expression. However, the effect of glutamine on BATF2 expression is shown only at the RNA level; important protein data are missing. All experiments related to glutamine were performed in murine macrophages. If the authors wish to claim that this mechanism allows tumor cells to downregulate BATF2, it is crucial to demonstrate that this regulation occurs in carcinoma cells and affects BATF2 protein levels. Furthermore, the effects of a glutamine diet on tumor growth following intratumoral injection of STING agonists appear to be relatively weak.”
Response 4: We appreciate this constructive comment. Because BATF2 is primarily expressed in epithelial cells and myeloid cells, we validated the impact of glutamine on BATF2 in both cell types. We additionally tested the effect of glutamine on the expression levels of BATF2 in THP1 cells. In agreement with mouse studies, we found that glutamine potently suppressed the mRNA expression levels of BATF2 and IFN-I target genes when THP1 cells were treated with cGAMP (New Supplementary Fig. 6a, Line 339-341). Then, we confirmed that glutamine potently inhibited the expression of BATF2 at protein levels and the production of IFN-b (New Supplementary Fig. 6b-c, Line 341-343). Similarly, we found that glutamine suppressed the expression of BATF2 at mRNA and protein levels in HNSCC cells (Supplementary Fig. 6d-e, Line 343-349).
To strengthen the in vivo data related to glutamine metabolism, we first repeated the glutamine diet experiment by including all groups in the same experiment for direct multi-comparisons. Consistent with the data presented in the original submission, CDA reduced tumor burden when mice were on a regular diet but failed to show any protection in mice on an isocaloric diet (New Fig. 5k, Line 374-377). We compared surrogate animal survival and found that CDA extended host survival only in the regular diet group New Supplementary Fig. 7g, Line 384-387). Glutamine-rich diet alone enhanced tumor growth at the baseline (Fig. 5k and New Supplementary Fig. 7g, Line 374-381 and 384-387). Then, we assessed the impact of inhibition of glutamine metabolism on tumor response to IFN-I agonists. In the same experiment shown in Fig. 5k, we also included two additional groups that received intra-tumoral injection of CDA and a glutaminase inhibitor, JHU083. One of these groups was on a regular diet, and the other was on an isocaloric glutamine-rich diet. Interestingly, although JHU083 did not further improve the anti-tumor efficacy of CDA in the regular diet group, it significantly improved tumor control in mice on a glutamine-rich diet (New Fig. 5l-m, Line 387-393). Overall, this series of new experiments substantiated the physiological relevance of the novel glutamine-BATF2-IFN-I pathway. Glutamine inhibits BATF2 at mRNA and protein levels, leading to dampened IFN-I production. A glutamine-rich diet desensitized tumors to STING stimulation and promoted tumor growth. Direct inhibition of glutamine metabolism more effectively reduced tumor burden in mice on a glutamine-rich diet.
5. “Comments on in vivo studies: In vivo experiments were conducted using different murine squamous cell carcinoma cell lines.there is no information about endogenous BATF2 protein expression in those cells. Figure 6f demonstrates reduced growth of Batf2-overexpressing tumors. To what extent this effect is related to STING activation remains unclear. Experiments should be performed using BATF2-overexpressing STING knockout cells. Additionally, survival curves should be included.”
Response 5: Thank you for the constructive comment. In our revised manuscript, we measured the endogenous levels of Batf2 in the mouse HNSCC cell lines MOC2-E6/E7, NOOC1, and NOOC2. MOC2-E6/E7 exhibited the lowest endogenous level of Batf2 expression, while NOOC2 showed high endogenous levels of Batf2 expression (New Supplementary Fig. 9a, Line 456-459). In addition to the Batf2-expressing MOC2-E6/E7 model we included in the original submission (Fig. 6), we generated new stable Batf2-deficient NOOC2 cells with its empty vector control (New Supplementary Fig. 9l, Line 523-525). In agreement with our previous findings, Batf2-deficient tumors grew significantly more aggressively (New Supplementary Fig. 9l-m, Line 523-526). Following this helpful suggestion, we also generated new vector control Batf2-expressing cell line and Sting-deficient, Batf2-expressing MOC2-E6/E7 cells. We found that cancer cell-specific Batf2-mediated tumor rejection completely depended on cancer cell expression of Sting because knocking down Sting abrogated Batf2-mediated protection (New Supplementary Fig. 9f-g, Line 471-477). We also included Kaplan-Meier survival analysis (New Supplementary Fig. 9g, Line 475-477). Please also refer to our response #3.
6. “In Figure 7: Is the enhanced growth of transplanted tumor cells in BATF2-/- mice due to the lack of STING activation?”
Response 6: Thank you for this thoughtful question. To examine the Sting pathway activation in Batf2-/- mice in vivo, we assessed the levels of Irf3 phosphorylation by flow cytometry and found that the proportion of p-Irf3+ cells in TILs from Batf2-/- mice was significantly lower than that in the control group using two different HNSCC models (New Fig. 7b and d, Line 533-542).
7. “Finally, the authors completely ignore relevant published data on BATF2 in cancer, even those studies which already showed that BATF2 has anti-tumor activity.”
Response 7: We appreciate the importance of published data. Thus, we revised the discussion to include these studies (Line 632-634). We also respectfully submit that our study has established the following novelties that effectively separate this study. (a) We thoroughly characterized a new molecular pathway that connects BATF2 with STING-specific IFN-I potentiation. We further strengthened the data to show that the S227 phosphorylation site is required for BATF2’s immune-activating function (please refer to details in our response to Reviewer 4 Comment #2). (b) We established a clear molecular mechanism of the BATF2-STING complex. Our new data identified the LBD domain of STING, which is essential for its oligomerization, as the critical binding site of BATF2 (please refer to details in our response to Reviewer #3 Comment #2). (c) We identified glutamine as a pivotal trans-regulatory element that suppresses the expression of BATF2. We characterized the impact of BATF2 on the metabolic activities of myeloid cells and established the role of glutamine in tumor response to IFN-I agonists. (d) Now we have shown that inhibition of glutamine metabolism did not further improve the anti-tumor efficacy of CDA in the regular diet group. However, inhibitors of glutamine metabolism significantly improved tumor control in mice on a glutamine-rich diet. (e) According to the 2025 Annual Report to the Nation on the Status of Cancer, oral cavity and pharynx cancer is one of the only three cancer types that showed a significant increase in incidence among both male and female patients. We created a rigorous new oral squamous cell carcinoma model NOOC2, which shows over 95% similarity in mutational signatures to human tobacco-associated cancers. None of the published studies was focused on the molecular biology of HNSCC. (f) We separately characterized the role of BATF2 in both epithelial and myeloid cell compartments, which are the principal cell types that express BATF2. None of the published studies examined the BATF2-IFN-I pathway in vivo. In addition, our new data show that BATF2-mediated tumor rejection depends on IFN-I signaling, Cxcl10, and cytotoxic T-cells. (g) We included complementary human specimen cohorts to substantiate the tumor-inhibitory function of BATF2. Our new data show that BATF2 levels were decreased as oral potentially malignant precursor lesions transformed and that BATF2 is associated with a favorable anti-tumor immune response profile.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author): with expertise in head and neck cancer, cancer immunology
“This manuscript offers a novel perspective on BATF2 as a glutamine-responsive tumor suppressor essential for promoting STING signaling and IFN-I production. The study is comprehensive, leveraging both molecular and preclinical models to delineate BATF2's immunomodulatory roles. However, some areas of the manuscript could benefit from additional clarification, experimental reinforcement, and broader context to enhance its impact and rigor.”
1. “Mechanistic Insight on Glutamine and Epigenetic Regulation: While the role of glutamine in promoting H3K27me3 modifications at the BATF2 promoter is well demonstrated, the study does not explore whether this mechanism also affects other key immune genes regulated by STING. A broader analysis of glutamine-induced epigenetic changes at loci relevant to the immune response (e.g., CXCL10 or IFN-I target genes) would strengthen the conclusion that glutamine broadly suppresses antitumor immunity through epigenetic remodeling.”
Response 1: Thank you for sharing this insight. In our original submission, we did include additional STING target genes, including Ifnb1 and Cxcl9 (Supplementary Fig. 6g, Line 354-358).
2. “Role of BATF2 in STING Oligomerization: The manuscript demonstrates that BATF2 is essential for STING oligomerization (Fig. 4h). However, the specific role of BATF2 in stabilizing these oligomers remains unclear. Testing whether BATF2 interacts directly with key regions of STING (e.g., using mutational analysis or co-immunoprecipitation of truncated STING constructs) would clarify the molecular basis of this interaction.”
Response 2: We appreciate this insightful comment. Following this recommendation, we generated new truncation mutants for STING. We deleted the N-terminus, the Ligand-Binding Domain, or the C-terminus of STING. All STING domain truncation mutants can be expressed. We immunoprecipitated HA-BATF2 and found that only the LBD domain was required for the BATF2-STING interaction (New Fig. 4i, Line 271-276). LBD is also the domain critical for STING oligomerization. Thus, it is likely that the BATF2-STING interaction stabilizes the STING oligomers in an LBD-dependent fashion.
3. “Function of CXCL10+ Myeloid Cells in Tumor Rejection: The authors highlight the expansion of CXCL10+ myeloid cells downstream of BATF2 but do not directly assess their functional relevance. Including depletion experiments (e.g., using neutralizing antibodies or conditional knockouts) to test whether CXCL10+ myeloid cells are necessary for BATF2-mediated tumor rejection would substantiate this claim.”
Response 3: Thank you for this thoughtful suggestion. We followed the advice and performed neutralization experiments. First, we administered 200 μg anti-Cxcl10 neutralizing antibody on day 7 after tumor implantation and continued 100 μg anti-Cxcl10 twice per week for a total of five doses. We found that Cxcl10 depletion abrogated Batf2-mediated protection (New Supplementary Fig. 9i, Line 505-510). We observed that T-cells from Batf2-expressing tumors showed significantly elevated effector function pathways, such as IFN-γ response, allograft rejection, IFN-α response, as well as cell proliferation, such as E2F targets, mitotic spindle, G2M checkpoint, and Myc targets (Fig. 6m). Thus, we then sought to determine whether Batf2-mediated protection depended on CD8+ T-cells. Our new data showed that anti-CD8-mediated T-cell depletion eliminated the protective effects of cancer cell-specific Batf2 expression (New Supplementary Fig. 9j, Line 510-515).
4. “Kinetics of BATF2 Expression and IFN-I Responses: The timing of BATF2 expression relative to IFN-I signaling and T-cell recruitment is critical to understanding its role in tumor immunity. Longitudinal studies tracking BATF2 expression, STING activation, and immune infiltration in tumors (e.g., via time-course RNA-Seq or flow cytometry) would provide valuable insights.”
Response 4: Thank you for raising this insightful point. We have now collected tumor specimens on days 7, 14, and 21 post-implantation of empty vector and Batf2-expressing tumors. Batf2-expressing tumors demonstrated a more favorable TME at the earliest time point, as evidenced by the early expansion of CD45+Tcr-CD11b+ myeloid cells that are positive phospho-Tbk1 and phospho-Irf3. Also noticeable at this early time point was the expansion of γδ T-cells. Then, at the later time points, Batf2-expressing tumors started to show significantly more CD8+ T-cells infiltration than control tumors, although this advantage appeared to become smaller as the tumor size continued to increase (New Fig. 6f-i, Line 477-488). These new data suggest that cancer cell-specific Batf2 expression reprograms innate and adaptive immune wiring in a stepwise fashion, with IFN-I activation in CD11b+ myeloid cells and γδ T-cells expansion as the earliest response feature, followed by expansion of CD8+ T-cells. In addition to the number difference in effectors, the quality of these T-cells is also different. As shown in our previous submission, the T-cells from Batf2-expressing tumors exhibited an Id2 effector signature with upregulated functional pathways, such as IFN-γ and proliferation responses (Fig. 6j-m).
5. “Relevance of p227 Phosphorylation Across Models: The phosphorylation of BATF2 at serine 227 (p227) is presented as critical for its function, but this claim is primarily demonstrated in vitro (Fig. 4k). Testing whether p227 phosphorylation is similarly required in vivo (e.g., using BATF2 p227A knock-in mice) would solidify this mechanistic insight.”
Response 5: Thank you for your thoughtful suggestion. Because our original and new data highlight the protective role of BATF2 in suppressing tumor initiation, here we substantiate the physiological relevance of serine 227 phosphorylation in vivo by generating new tumor models that stably express empty vector, wild-type Batf2, and 227A mutant Batf2. In agreement with our other data, expression of Batf2 inhibited tumor growth. However, Batf2-mediated protection was abrogated by mutating serine 227 to alanine and disabling phosphorylation at this amino acid (New Supplementary Fig. 9n, Line 526-531). Hence, here we show that the phosphorylation of S227 is critical for the tumor inhibitor role of Batf2 in vivo.
6. “STING Agonist Resistance and Glutamine Levels: The manuscript concludes that high glutamine levels blunt STING agonist efficacy (Fig. 5). It would be helpful to explore whether glutamine-targeting interventions (e.g., glutaminase inhibitors) can rescue STING agonist responses in glutamine-rich conditions, thus supporting potential combination therapies.”
Response 6: Taking this helpful advice to heart, we performed new in vivo experiments to substantiate the physiological relevance of the glutamine-BATF2-IFN-I pathway. In our original submission, we showed that a selective glutaminase inhibitor, Bis-2-(5-phenylacetamido-1,3,4-thiadiazol-2-yl)ethyl sulfide (BPTES), significantly elevated the expression levels of Batf2, Ifnb1, and pan-Ifna in BMDM under STING-stimulated conditions (Fig. 5c-d and Supplementary Fig. 5g-h). To strengthen the in vivo data related to glutamine metabolism, we first repeated the glutamine diet experiment by including all groups in the same experiment for direct comparisons. Consistent with the data presented in the original submission, CDA reduced tumor burden when mice were on a regular diet but failed to show any protection in mice on an isocaloric diet (New Fig. 5k, Line 374-377). We compared surrogate animal survival and found that CDA extended host survival only in the regular diet group (New Supplementary Fig. 7g, Line 384-387). Glutamine-rich diet alone enhanced tumor growth at the baseline (New Fig. 5k and New Supplementary Fig. 7g, Line 374-387). Then, we assessed the impact of inhibition of glutamine metabolism on tumor response to IFN-I agonists. In the same experiment shown in Fig. 5k, we also have two additional groups that received intra-tumoral injection of CDA and a glutaminase inhibitor, JHU083. One of these groups was on a regular diet, and the other was on an isocaloric glutamine-rich diet. Interestingly, although JHU083 did not further improve the anti-tumor efficacy of CDA in the regular diet group, it significantly improved CDA-mediated tumor control in mice on a glutamine-rich diet (New Fig. 5l-m, Line 387-393). Overall, this series of new experiments substantiated the physiological relevance of the novel glutamine-BATF2-IFN-I pathway. Glutamine inhibits BATF2 at mRNA and protein levels, leading to dampened IFN-I production. A glutamine-rich diet desensitized tumors to STING stimulation and promoted tumor growth. Direct inhibition of glutamine metabolism more effectively reduced tumor burden in mice on a glutamine-rich diet.
7. “BATF2 in Human Clinical Samples: While BATF2 expression is correlated with immune markers in HNSCC patient datasets, there is little exploration of its prognostic or therapeutic relevance. Analyzing BATF2 expression in patients stratified by clinical outcomes (e.g., response to immunotherapy) would provide translational significance to the findings.”
Response 7: Thank you for sharing this important insight. To strengthen human specimen studies, we included new analyses using three additional independent cohorts of clinical specimens. A common caveat of analyzing human oral potentially malignant disorders (OPMD) specimens is the often lack of longitudinal monitoring, where leukoplakia of unknown malignant transformation potential is included. To substantiate the role of BATF2 in suppressing tumor initiation, we first identified patients who had OPMD progressing into HNSCC despite complete surgical removal of the OPMD. We performed BATF2 staining on the paired longitudinal specimens and found that BATF2 expression levels were lower in paired HNSCC than in OPMD (New Fig. 1f-g, Line 161-163).
Next, to directly assess whether BATF2 in fresh human oral squamous cell carcinoma specimens regulates their response to IFN agonists, we procured fresh human oral squamous cell carcinomas from eight patients. We trisected the tissue into three pieces of comparable size. The first piece was injected with PBS ex vivo, the second piece was injected with 5.0 μg CDA, and the third piece was formalin fixed and integrated into a tissue microarray (Fig. 1h, Line 163-168). We performed qPCR using tissue homogenates and normalized the levels of IFNB1 by PTPRC, the latter of which encodes CD45. We quantified BATF2 staining using Aperio Imagescope and generated BATF2 scores. Then, we performed a Spearman correlation analysis between BATF2 scores and normalized IFNB1 expression and identified a strong positive correlation between BATF2 and STING response with a r-value of 0.86 (**p<0.01) (New Fig. 1i, Line 168-172).
To comprehensively assess the impact of BATF2 on overall survival, we resorted to five TCGA data sets that include HNSCC (n=522, *p=0.034), high-grade serous carcinoma (OV, n=303, *p=0.0181), sarcoma (SARC, n=260, *p=0.0208), skin cutaneous melanoma (SKCM, n=471, **p=0.00106), and stomach adenocarcinoma (STAD, n=415, *p=0.0428). We found that higher expression levels of BATF2 were positively correlated with patient outcomes (Supplementary Fig. 1e-i, Line 154-158). The HNSCC TCGA data set does not have responder status for immunotherapy. Thus, we next examined four data sets that contained responder status to anti-PD1. We found that the responders among patients with STAD (****p<0.0001), SKCM (****p<0.0001), bladder squamous cell carcinoma (BLCA, *p=0.02), or non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC, ****p<0.0001) showed significantly higher levels of BATF2 expression than non-responders (New Supplementary Fig. 1j-m, Line 173-177). Overall, this analysis shows that BATF2 promotes anti-tumor immune responses in tumor types besides HNSCC.
Minor Revisions
Terminology Consistency: Standardize terms like “IFN-I signature genes” and “IFN-I target genes” for clarity.
Response: We changed all “IFN-I signature genes” to “IFN-I target genes”.
Text Clarity: Simplify the introduction by focusing on BATF2’s novelty in immune modulation while reducing background repetition.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author): with expertise in cancer immunology, metabolism
1. “The manuscript establishes a role for BATF2 as a tumor suppressor gene in HNSCC and combines data from human tumor samples and several mouse models. Robust genetic approaches and state-of-the-art read-outs are used to support the findings. The results are well-described, and the figures and figure legends are nicely presented. The role of BATF2 as a tumor suppressor gene is well established by previous studies, including in epithelial cancers: PMID 26135942, 32650804, 37995570, 34778372 and more. Some of these studies show, similarly to the current one, that BATF2 expression on tumor cells shapes the TME immune infiltrate. The role of BATF2 in driving inflammatory responses, e.g. in macrophages, has also been previously observed: PMID 25957166 and others. The current study presents novel points on the importance of BATF2 for type I IFN responses following STING, but not MAVS activation, in particular on the phosphorylation of BATF at serine 227 as a prerequisite for interaction with STING. A further novel point is the metabolic regulation of BATF2 expression through glutamine. However, I think that, in particular, the last point needs to be investigated in greater detail.”
Response 1: Thank you for your thoughtful comments and for recognizing the novel aspects of this study. We have revised our discussion to recognize the previous literature more broadly. We also respectfully submit that our study has established the following novelties that effectively separate this study. (a) We thoroughly characterized a new molecular pathway that connects BATF2 with STING-specific IFN-I potentiation. We further strengthened the data to show that the S227 phosphorylation site is required for BATF2’s immune-activating function (please refer to details in our response to Reviewer 4 Comment #2). (b) We established a clear molecular mechanism of the BATF2-STING complex. Our new data identified the LBD domain of STING, which is essential for its oligomerization, as the critical binding site of BATF2 (please refer to details in our response to Reviewer #3 Comment #2). (c) We identified glutamine as a pivotal trans-regulatory element that suppresses the expression of BATF2. We characterized the impact of BATF2 on the metabolic activities of myeloid cells and established the role of glutamine in tumor response to IFN-I agonists. (d) Now we have shown that inhibition of glutamine metabolism did not further improve the anti-tumor efficacy of CDA in the regular diet group. However, inhibitors of glutamine metabolism significantly improved CDA-mediated tumor control in mice on a glutamine-rich diet. (e) According to the 2025 Annual Report to the Nation on the Status of Cancer, oral cavity and pharynx cancer is one of the only three cancer types that showed a significant increase in incidence among both male and female patients. We created a rigorous new oral squamous cell carcinoma model NOOC2, which shows over 95% similarity in mutational signatures to human tobacco-associated cancers. None of the published studies was focused on the molecular biology of HNSCC. (f) We separately characterized the role of BATF2 in both epithelial and myeloid cell compartments, which are the principal cell types that express BATF2. None of the published studies examined the BATF2-IFN-I pathway in vivo. In addition, our new data show that BATF2-mediated tumor rejection depends on IFN-I signaling, Cxcl10, and cytotoxic T-cells. (g) We included complementary human specimen cohorts to substantiate the tumor-inhibitory function of BATF2. Our new data show that BATF2 levels were decreased as oral potentially malignant precursor lesions transformed and that BATF2 is associated with a favorable anti-tumor immune response profile.
To substantiate the physiological relevance of serine 227 phosphorylation in vivo, we generated new tumor models that stably express empty vector, wild-type Batf2, and 227A mutant Batf2. In agreement with our other data, expression of Batf2 inhibited tumor growth. However, Batf2-mediated protection was completely abrogated by mutating serine 227 to alanine and disabling phosphorylation at this amino acid (New Supplementary Fig. 9n, Line 526-531). Hence, here we show that the phosphorylation of S227 is critical for the tumor inhibitor role of Batf2 in vivo.
We also performed additional experiments to strengthen the glutamine-BATF2-IFN-I signaling axis. Because BATF2 is primarily expressed in epithelial cells and myeloid cells, we validated the impact of glutamine on BATF2 in both cell types. In our original submission, we showed the inhibitory effect of glutamine on the BATF2 protein levels (Fig. 5g). During the revision, we additionally tested the effect of glutamine on the expression levels of BATF2 in THP1 cells. In agreement with mouse studies, we found that glutamine potently suppressed the mRNA expression levels of BATF2 and IFN-I target genes when THP1 cells were treated with cGAMP (New Supplementary Fig. 6a, Line 339-341). Then, we confirmed that glutamine potently inhibited the expression of BATF2 at protein levels and the production of IFN-b (Supplementary Fig. 6b-c, Line 341-343). Similarly, we found that glutamine suppressed the expression of BATF2 at mRNA and protein levels in HNSCC cells (New Supplementary Fig. 6d-e, Line 343-349).
To strengthen the in vivo data related to glutamine metabolism, we first repeated the glutamine diet experiment by including all groups in the same experiment for direct multi-comparisons. Consistent with the data presented in the original submission, CDA reduced tumor burden when mice were on a regular diet but failed to show any protection in mice on an isocaloric diet (New Fig. 5k, Line 381-387). We compared surrogate animal survival and found that CDA extended host survival only in the regular diet group (New Supplementary Fig. 7g, Line 381-387). Glutamine-rich diet alone enhanced tumor growth at the baseline (New Fig. 5k and New Supplementary Fig. 7g, Line 374-387). In addition, we implanted the same tumor model that showed more aggressive growth in wild-type mice on a glutamine-rich diet into Batf2-/- mice on either a regular diet or an isocaloric, glutamine-rich diet. We found that a glutamine-rich diet could no longer promote tumor growth in the absence of host expression of Batf2 (Supplementary Fig. 7f, Line 377-381), suggesting that glutamine-mediated tumor aggression depends on its suppression of Batf2. Then, we assessed the impact of inhibition of glutamine metabolism on tumor response to IFN-I agonists. In the same experiment shown in Fig. 5k, we also have two additional groups that received intra-tumoral injection of CDA and a glutaminase inhibitor, JHU083. One of these groups was on a regular diet, and the other was on an isocaloric glutamine-rich diet. Interestingly, although JHU083 did not further improve the anti-tumor efficacy of free CDA in the regular diet group, it significantly improved tumor control in mice on a glutamine-rich diet (New Fig. 5l-m, Line 387-393). Overall, this series of new experiments substantiated the physiological relevance of the novel glutamine-BATF2-IFN-I pathway. Glutamine inhibits BATF2 at mRNA and protein levels, leading to dampened IFN-I production. A glutamine-rich diet desensitized tumors to STING stimulation and promoted tumor growth. Direct inhibition of glutamine metabolism more effectively reduced tumor burden in mice on a glutamine-rich diet.
“Major points:”
2. “The manuscript is somewhat difficult to follow, as the authors frequently switch between the role of BATF2 in BMDM and in tumor cells. In the end, it doesn't really become clear to me whether BATF2 expression on one of these two populations is more important for the observed in vivo effects. Also, not all mechanisms are shown in both cell types. The interaction of STING and phosphorylation of BATF2 are shown in tumor cell lines, while the regulation of BATF2 through glutamine is shown in BMDM.”
Response 2: We appreciate the thoughtful comment. The reason we focused on two cell compartments is that BATF2 is most highly expressed in epithelial/carcinoma cells and myeloid cells. We established a novel glutamine-BATF2-STING pathway that determines HNSCC immunogenicity. We agree that thoroughly testing the key mechanisms in both compartments improves the rigor. First, we extended the testing for the interaction between BATF2 and STING from HEK-293T cells and the HNSCC cells to macrophages. We immunoprecipitated BATF2 and blotted STING to confirm such interaction (New Fig. 4h, Line 269-271). Then, we further refined the mechanism of the BATF2-STING binding by mapping the domain requirements for this interaction. We generated new STING mutants with the deletion of the N-terminus, the Ligand-Binding Domain, or the C-terminus. All STING domain truncation mutants can be expressed. We immunoprecipitated HA-BATF2 and found that only the LBD domain was required for the BATF2-STING interaction (New Fig. 4i, Line 271-276). LBD is also the domain critical for STING oligomerization. Thus, it is likely that the BATF2-STING interaction stabilizes the STING oligomers in an LBD-dependent fashion. Next, we confirmed the critical role of S227 phosphorylation in HNSCC cells. In our original submission, we showed that the BATF2 S227A mutant failed to reconstitute STING activation in Batf2-/- BMDM. During the revision, we performed new experiments to show that the expression of full-length BATF2 restored cGAMP-induced IFN-I response in an HNSCC cell line that is otherwise non-responsive to cGAMP transfection. Notably, the BATF2 S227A mutant abrogated the role of BATF2-mediated STING activation (New Supplementary Fig. 4h, Line 308-311). Then, we additionally tested the effect of glutamine on the expression levels of BATF2 in THP1 cells. In agreement with mouse studies, we found that glutamine potently suppressed the mRNA expression levels of BATF2 and IFN-I target genes when THP1 cells were treated with cGAMP (Supplementary Fig. 6a, Line 339-341). Then, we confirmed that glutamine potently inhibited the expression of BATF2 at protein levels and the production of IFN-b (New Supplementary Fig. 6b-c, Line 341-343). Similarly, we found that glutamine suppressed the expression of BATF2 at mRNA and protein levels in HNSCC cells (New Supplementary Fig. 6d-e, Line 343-349) (Please also refer to our response to Reviewer 4 Comment 1).
3. I find the beginning of the paper confusing. The authors begin the manuscript with the question why HPV+ HNSCC do not respond to ICI blockade as well as expected and compare single-cell transcriptomes from HPV+ and HPV- patients to discover aberrations in the immune cell population composition. However, there is no correlation with clinical responses to ICI, which makes me wonder why this comparison was made in the first place. I personally think that leading into the paper by stating that high BATF2 expression was found in clusters 10, 19, 20 which also had high type I IFN gene expression would make a clearer point, and that splitting the samples in HPV+ and HPV- doesn't have an added value for the manuscript.
Response 3: We appreciate the suggestion and de-emphasized the HPV-related immune escape mechanism to focus on the link between BATF2 and IFN-I target genes in the Introduction section.
4. “The interaction between BATF2 and STING is shown for tumor cells, but not for macrophages. Do the authors have evidence that the same mechanism is active in macrophages? Vice versa, does glutamine concentration in the media affect the BATF2 expression in tumor cells, or only in macrophages?”
Response 4: Thank you for this thoughtful suggestion. In our revised manuscript, we performed new experiments and validated the mechanism in both tumor cells and BMDM (New Supplementary Fig. 6a-e, Line 339-349). Please also see our response to Reviewer 4 Comment 1.
5. “How much of the effects of high-glutamine media on type I IFN secretion is mediated through BATF2? The experiments in Fig. 5e-f should be repeated with BATF2-/- cells. Along the same lines, is the effect of glutamine-rich diet on tumor development in Fig. 5k-q mediated solely through BATF2? Experiments should include groups with BATF2 KO tumors and/or hosts as controls.”
Response 5: Thank you for raising this thoughtful point. We additionally evaluated whether glutamine-mediated STING suppression depended on Batf2. We cultured Batf2-/- BMDM in media containing 0 g/L, 0.5 g/L, or 5.0 g/L glutamine for 24 hours, followed by transfection with 3.0 µg/mL ISD for 16 hours. Notably, we did not observe a reduction in the protein levels of Ifn-b in the supernatant when glutamine was added to the culture compared with glutamine-free control (New Supplementary Fig. 6f, Line 349-353), suggesting that Batf2 is indispensable for glutamine-mediated STING inhibition. In addition, we implanted the same tumor model that showed more aggressive growth in wild-type mice on a glutamine-rich diet into Batf2-/- mice on either a regular diet or an isocaloric, glutamine-rich diet. We found that a glutamine-rich diet could no longer promote tumor growth in the absence of host expression of Batf2 (Supplementary Fig. 7f, Line 377-381).
6. “What is the mechanism by which glutamine epigenetically regulates BATF2? Is this mediated through glutamine itself, or through some of its downstream metabolites, e.g. alpha-ketoglutarate. How are the metabolic profiles with increased oxidative phosphorylation (Figure 5i-j) related to the remaining mechanism? Would other metabolic conditions that increase OCR also affect BATF2 expression, or is this specific to glutamine-rich media?”
Response 6: Thank you for those thoughtful questions. Previous studies have shown that IL4 treatment, which promotes the M2-like alternative activation of macrophages, reduces the deposition of H3K27me3 on the promoters of Arg1, Ym1, Retnla, and Mrc1 genes. This finding is conceptually in agreement with our data, which show that glutamine potentiates an OCR profile conducive to M2-like alternative activation and promotes the deposition of repressive H3K27m3 on the promoters of Batf2, Ifnb1, and Cxcl9. EZH2 is a key enzyme that methylates H3K27. Recent studies show that inhibition of EZH2 potentiates type-I interferons, which supports this mechanistic link. We revised our discussion to include these future directions (Line 613-621). To test whether amino acids-potentiated suppression of BATF2 is specific to glutamine, we tested a panel of essential and non-essential amino acids. We cultured UMSCC108 cells in complete media and media specifically deficient only in one amino acid and tested the levels of BATF2. In agreement with the data presented in the original submission, glutamine deficiency resulted in higher levels of BATF2. Interestingly, we also found that tyrosine, valine, isoleucine, and methionine also suppress BATF2. None of the other non-essential and essential amino acids regulates BATF2, suggesting pathway specificity (New Supplementary Fig. 5a, Line 313-318). A recent study showed that methionine restriction increases the STING pathway activation, conceptually in agreement with our finding that methionine suppresses BATF2 (Line 629-631).
7. “Are there data from human tumor samples supporting the notion that glutamine metabolism regulates BATF2-expression?”
Response 7: Thank you for this insightful suggestion. To address this question, we collected fresh oral squamous cell carcinoma tissue from 15 patients and performed bulk RNA-Seq. Then, we performed a correlation analysis between BATF2 and glutamine metabolism markers. We also included IFN-I target genes as controls. We found that BATF2 is strongly positively correlated with Th1 genes, including CXCL9, CXCL10, ISG15, IFNB1, OASL, and TNF. Notably, we also found that BATF2 is inversely correlated with glutamine metabolism pathway genes, such as SLC7A5, SLC1A5, SLC38A2 and GLS. In agreement, the Th1 cytokines, including IFNG, IFNB1, and TNF, all show an inverse correlation with glutamine metabolism (New Fig. 5r, Line 424-432). These new human data support the glutamine-BATF2-IFN pathway we characterized in depth in this study.
8. “Figure 6: are only gd T cells responsible for the rejection of BATF2-expressing tumors? I would be interested to see experiments with depletion of alpha-beta T cells, especially as these subsets are also affected by BATF2 expression in other figures. Vice versa, are gd T cells affected in the tumor models presented in Fig. 7?”
Response 8: Thank you for this insightful suggestion. We have now collected tumor specimens on days 7, 14, and 21 post-implantation of empty vector and Batf2-expressing tumors to determine the dynamics of the infiltration of γδ T-cells and ab T-cells. Batf2-expressing tumors demonstrated a more favorable TME at the earliest time point, as evidenced by the early expansion of CD45+Tcr-CD11b+ myeloid cells that are positive phospho-Tbk1 and phospho-Irf3. Also noticeable at this early time point was the expansion of γδ T-cells. Then, at the later time points, Batf2-expressing tumors started to show significantly more CD8+ T-cells infiltration than control tumors, although this advantage appeared to become smaller as the tumor size continued to increase (New Fig. 6f-i, Line 477-485). These new data suggest that cancer cell-specific Batf2 expression reprograms innate and adaptive immune wiring in a stepwise fashion, with IFN-I activation in CD11b+ myeloid cells and γδ T-cells expansion as the earliest response feature, followed by expansion of CD8+ T-cells. In our original submission, we observed that pooled γδ T-cells and ab T-cells from Batf2-expressing tumors showed significantly elevated effector function pathways, such as IFN-γ response, allograft rejection, IFN-α response, as well as cell proliferation, such as E2F targets, mitotic spindle, G2M checkpoint, and Myc targets (Fig. 6m). Thus, we then sought to determine whether Batf2-mediated protection depended on CD8+ T-cells. Our new data showed that anti-CD8-mediated T-cell depletion eliminated the protective effects of cancer cell-specific Batf2 expression (New Supplementary Fig. 9j, Line 510-515). Next, we evaluated whether host Batf2 expression has an impact on γδ T-cell infiltration into the TME. We stained tumors grown in wild-type and Batf2-/- mice with a δ-TCR-specific antibody and found that there were fewer γδ T-cells in tumors grown in Batf2-/- mice (New Supplementary Fig. 10a, Line 537-538).
9. “It would be interesting to know if BATF2 expression by tumor cells drives only local or also systemic immune responses. For example, the authors could use the model in FIgure 6f and inject WT tumor cells in one flank and BATF2-expressing or WT cells in the other flank, and monitor whether the presence of a BATF2-expressing tumor activates a systemic immune response leading to a better control of the WT tumor in the other flank, compared to animals bearing WT tumors on both sides.”
Response 9: We appreciate this thoughtful advice to examine the abscopal effects. We implanted the empty vector (EV) control and Batf2-expressing tumors on the right flank. As expected, we observed a significant reduction in tumor volume when Batf2 was expressed. However, the EV control tumors grown in the left flank of mice that bear Batf2-expressing tumors in the right flank did not show a difference in volume compared to those EV tumors grown in the left flank of mice that bear EV tumors in the right flank (New Supplementary Fig. 9k, Line 515-522). These data suggest that the BATF2-expressing tumors establish a favorable local TME without triggering a notable abscopal effect.
10. “Would BATF2-expressing tumors grow more aggressively if mice are kept on a glutamine-rich diet (Figure 6)?”
Response 10: Thank you for this question. We first repeated the diet experiment so that all treatment groups could be monitored simultaneously. In the non-treated empty vector tumor groups, isocaloric glutamine-rich diet alone was sufficient to result in higher tumor burdens (New Fig. 5m, Line 374-377). Because the stable overexpression of Batf2 cannot be silenced by a glutamine-rich diet, we did not observe a difference in the tumor burden of Batf2-expressing tumors between regular and a glutamine-rich diet. To assess whether glutamine-mediated tumor aggression depends on the suppression of Batf2, we implanted the same tumor model that showed more aggressive growth in wild-type mice on a glutamine-rich diet into Batf2-/- mice on either a regular diet or an isocaloric, glutamine-rich diet. We found that a glutamine-rich diet could no longer promote tumor growth in the absence of host expression of Batf2 (Supplementary Fig. 7f, Line 377-381) (please also refer to our response to Reviewer 4 Comment 5).
11. “Is there a possibility to target BATF2 or any downstream gene pharmacologically?”
Response 11: Thank you for this thoughtful advice. To target the glutamine-BATF2 pathway pharmacologically, we assessed the impact of inhibition of glutamine metabolism on tumor response to IFN-I agonists. In the same experiment shown in Fig. 5k, we also have two additional groups that received intra-tumoral injection of CDA and a glutaminase inhibitor, JHU083. One of these groups was on a regular diet, and the other was on an isocaloric glutamine-rich diet. Interestingly, although JHU083 did not further improve the anti-tumor efficacy of CDA in the regular diet group, it significantly improved tumor control in mice on a glutamine-rich diet (New Fig. 5l-m, Line 387-393). Please also refer to our response to Reviewer 4 Comment 1.
12. “Minor points:
I would recommend to include in the figure legends how often experiments were performed and whether pooled or representative data are shown.”
Response 12: Thank you for the advice. We have revised the figure legends to include these details.
13. “Why are cells sometimes stimulated with ISD/cGAMP, and other times with STING?”
Response 13: Thank you for your careful review. In most cases, we transfected cGAMP or ISD in BMDM to activate STING and overexpress STING in HNSCC cells to activate the pathway. We and others have shown that cancer cells have evolved multiple mechanisms to suppress the STING-TBK1-IFN pathway, such as promoting the turnover of STING and sequestering STING away from interacting with TBK1. This pathway is central for the immune sensing of HNSCC, which is likely why the tumors need multiple mechanisms to dampen this pathway. The regulation of this pathway is highly relevant for the following reasons. (a) During tumor initiation, when immune surveillance determines the outcomes of epithelial transformation, the proper activation of the innate immune pathways enables the maturation of antigen-presenting cells and subsequent cross-priming of T-cells. Known oncogenes for HNSCC, such as SOX2 and HPV16 E7, potently shut down IFN-I production. To evaluate whether BATF2 helps to launch the IFN-I pathway before epithelial malignant transformation, we expressed BATF2 in normal oral epithelial NOM9-TK cells, which directly triggered the phosphorylation of TBK1 and STING, indicative of pathway activation (New Supplementary Fig. 3d, Line 234-240). (b) In murine HNSCC cells, high Batf2 expression was also associated with elevated transcription levels of IFNb1 (New Supplementary Fig. 9a and 9l, Line 456-459 and 523-525). In our previous submission, we showed that Batf2-expressing tumors are much more immunogenic (Fig. 6). To substantiate the physiological relevance of the Batf2-Sting pathway, we generated additional stable cell lines, including vector-controlled Batf2-expressing and Batf2-expressing, Sting-deficient tumor cells. We found that cancer cell-specific Batf2-mediated tumor rejection depended on cancer cell expression of Sting because knocking down Sting abrogated Batf2-mediated protection (New Supplementary Fig. 9f-g, Line 473-477). (c) Now we also show that HNSCC cells only showed a modest increase in the phosphorylation of TBK1 and STING with cGAMP transfection. However, the STING response was largely restored when we expressed BATF2 (New Supplementary Fig. 4h, Line 308-311).
14. “The discussion is quite short and could be extended to interpret the findings in the light of other relevant studies in the field.”
Response 14: We have revised the discussion section.
POINT-BY-POINT RESPONSE TO REVIEWERS’ COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
“The authors have suitably addressed my previous minor concerns, and their report is significantly improved.”
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s enthusiastic feedback and the insightful comments that helped us to improve the quality of this manuscript.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
“The authors adequately addressed the major points I raised.
Minor: Some figure panels are quite dense, for example, Fig. 2D-L. The colour code does not need to be repeated in every graph; the same applies to Fig. 3A–D.”
Response:
We thank the reviewer for the enthusiastic feedback regarding the figure presentation. Following the reviewer’s advice, we have simplified the figures by reducing panel density and avoiding unnecessary repetition of the colour code. Specifically, the colour legend is now shown only once for each group of related panels (e.g., Fig. 2D–L and Fig. 3A–D), which improves clarity and readability.
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
“The authors present a substantially revised manuscript and have answered my questions. I don't have further comments.”
Response:
We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comments that helped us to improve the breadth and depth of this study.

## Abstract

Recent evidence highlights the significance of a new type of tumour suppressors, which are not frequently mutated but inhibited by metabolic cues in cancers. Here, we identify BATF2 as a tumour suppressor whose expression is epigenetically silenced by glutamine in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinomas (HNSCC). BATF2 correlates with type-I interferon and Th1 signatures in human HNSCC, with correlation coefficients even stronger than those of the positive control, STING. The phosphorylation of BATF2 at serine 227 promotes the oligomerization of STING. BATF2 deficiency or high glutamine levels result in higher oxygen consumption rates and metabolic profiles unfavorable for type-I interferon production. An isocaloric glutamine-rich diet abolishes STING-mediated effector cell expansion in tumours, weakening STING agonist-induced tumour control. Cancer cell-specific BATF2 expression promotes an Id2-centered T-cell effector signature, reduces T-cell exhaustion, and triggers spontaneous HNSCC rejection in a type-I interferon-dependent fashion. Utilizing syngeneic subcutaneous, orthotopic, and 24-week-long cigarette smoke carcinogen-induced HNSCC models, we demonstrate that host Batf2 deficiency results in increased infiltration of CD206+ myeloid cells and reduced effector CD8+ T-cells, accelerating the initiation of cancers. Overall, we reveal a tumour suppressor BATF2 whose loss is mediated by unique metabolic cues in the TME and drives cancer immune escape.

---

## Introduction

The clinical success of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) proves that cancers can be separated from the normal tissue in which they arise by the immune system. The tumour mutational burden has been extensively characterized to test the hypothesis that the number of tumour-specific antigens underpins the immunogenicity of cancers. Recognizing the evidence substantiating this theory in several cancer types, some cancers with modest responses to ICI, however, harbor high mutational loads1. To understand the mechanism governing the immunogenicity of these cancers, we employed head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) as a model. Two distinct sets of etiological factors drive HNSCC initiation and both subsets contain high and similar levels of mutational burdens2. The human papillomavirus (HPV)-negative HNSCC is associated with cigarette smoke and heavy alcohol consumption. The HPV+ HNSCC often occurs in the Waldeyer’s ring, where lymphoid structures are enriched. Gleaning evidence from two large cohorts of patients with HNSCC, we found that the Stimulator of Interferon Genes (STING)–type-I interferon (IFN-I) pathway underpins the immunogenicity of HNSCC. Oncogenes, high-risk HPV and metabolic conditions can all dampen STING response3–5. Recent structural evidence shows that STING functions by assembling into large multimeric protein complexes6. Despite the clear delineation of the canonical STING-TANK Binding Kinase 1 (TBK1)-Interferon Regulatory Factor 3 (IRF3) signaling axis, key components in the STING complex contributing to cancer immune surveillance remain to be discovered.

Here, we show that Basic Leucine Zipper ATF-Like Transcription Factor 2 (BATF2) functions as a tumour suppressor by sustaining the fitness of STING. BATF2 is indispensable for the activation of the STING pathway and not required for cytoplasmic dsRNA-mediated IFN-I activation. BATF2 translocates to endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-associated membranes upon STING stimulation and interacts with STING. We identify Serine 227 as a critical site for phosphorylation during BATF2 activation. High glutamine levels suppress the expression of BATF2 epigenetically and elevate oxidative phosphorylation to dampen IFN-I responses. BATF2 expression leads to IFN-I and γδ T-cell-dependent HNSCC rejection. A deficiency in BATF2 results in the expedited onset of cigarette smoke carcinogen-induced HNSCC with infiltration of increased M2-like macrophages and decreased Th1 effector cells. Using human HNSCC specimens, we show that high levels of BATF2 correlate with increased CD8+ T-cell infiltration and that glutamine metabolism is inversely correlated with BATF2-IFN-I signatures.
